newsitem.title: UK: MEPC increased profit hit by exceptional.
newsitem.headline: MEPC increased profit hit by exceptional.

text.p: British property group MEPC on Tuesday reported increased first half pre-tax profits of 75.7 million pounds ($124 million) which were all but wiped out by an exceptional charge.
But by cancelling sterling interest rate swap agreements at a cost of 73.2 million pounds MEPC said it had substantially reduced future costs and predicted increased dividends for 1998 and beyond.
There was a subdued reaction in the market to the news. MEPC shares were down just a penny at 514.5 pence at 0945 GMT.
MEPC chief executive James Tuckey told Reuters the group was well positioned to make the most of a market which was moving in its favour, although he warned there were signs of overheating.

And while dismissing recent takeover talk surrounding MEPC, Tuckey said he would not be doing his duty to shareholders if he did not treat any approaches seriously, although he admitted the fall-out following the talks had been a distraction.
He said the firm, which in March announced it had ended merger talks with smaller rival Hammerson, was not talking to anyone at the moment and did not anticipate doing so.
MEPC said the scale of benefits from a merger with Hammerson would have been small and the financial effect would have diluted its earnings per share and reduced the dividends for its shareholders.

The group said it would maintain its dividend at 20 pence per share for 1997, announcing a maintained interim dividend of 5.25 pence. But it said the cancellation of the swap agreements would improve dividend cover in 1998 and subsequent years.
Tuckey said MEPC had made management changes, refocused its portfolio, reduced its debt cost and had a modest development programme in the pipeline.
"Its been an extremely active six months and we feel pretty confident with the outlook," he said.
But while he sees the property market continuing to improve for the next 18-24 months, Tuckey said he was acutely aware of its cyclical nature.
"A correction will come and we need to be prepared," he said. It was a legitimate question to ask if the market was overheating, he added.
The easy availability of credit from both British and overseas banks was a key factor in this, and one which banks needed to be wary of, Tuckey said.
Despite this caution, MEPC is involved in a development programme with over 300 million pounds of expenditure still to come in the next few years.
The firm has 164 million pounds for purchases and development in the pipeline for the second half.
While much of this is directed at the British market, particularly the leisure sector, MEPC also has schemes underway in Dallas in the U.S. and Brisbane, Australia.
Tuckey said he did not know if there was a "big deal" likely in the British property company sector but based on MEPC's experience of its talks with Hammerson, any likely cost savings were not great.
It was probably more correct to direct talk of rationalisation to the smaller companies, where cost savings might be greater, he added.
